result.summary: Perseus turns the scoffing king Polydectes to stone with Medusa's head. Minerva then visits the Muses on Helicon to see the spring made by Pegasus. Urania tells how Pyreneus tried to assault the Muses and died, and how the Pierides were defeated in a singing contest and turned into magpies, before Calliope rises to sing.

scenes.title: Polydectes turned to stone
scenes.summary: Polydectes denies that Medusa is dead. Perseus warns the onlookers to shut their eyes and turns the king to stone with Medusa's head.
scenes.stakes: Polydectes risks his life by mocking Perseus; Perseus's honor is doubted.

scenes.title: Minerva visits Helicon
scenes.summary: Minerva leaves Perseus and flies to Helicon to see the spring that Pegasus opened. Urania welcomes her and shows her the groves, and a Muse begins to speak of her fears.

scenes.title: The Muses and Pyreneus
scenes.summary: A Muse tells how Pyreneus lured them into his house in the rain and tried to force them. They escaped by flight, and he leapt from his tower to his death.
scenes.stakes: The Muses faced violence from Pyreneus; he died in the fall.

scenes.title: The magpies on the boughs
scenes.summary: Minerva hears voices and discovers nine magpies. Urania explains they are the defeated daughters of Pierus and Evippe.

scenes.title: The Pierides' challenge and song
scenes.summary: The nine sisters challenge the Muses, and the Nymphs judge. The first Pierid sings of Typhoeus and the gods hiding in animal forms in Egypt.
scenes.stakes: The loser must give up its home ground: the Muses the spring, the Pierides the Emathian plains.

scenes.title: Calliope rises to sing
scenes.summary: Minerva asks to hear the Muses' song. Calliope is chosen and begins to sing.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Minerva, also called Pallas.
Libyan Ammon is the ram-horned form of Jupiter.

notable_quotes.reason: Pyreneus's boast leads directly to his fatal leap from the tower.

analysis.text: Disbelief and arrogance are punished: Polydectes is petrified, Pyreneus dies, and the Pierides lose their human form.
The Pierid song of gods hiding as animals reflects Greek and Roman interpretations of Egyptian animal-headed gods.

legacy.text: The spring Hippocrene made by Pegasus became a standard poetic symbol of inspiration.

fun_facts.text: The Latin word for magpie, pica, is the source of the English word pie in magpie's name through Old French, and of the printing term pica.

language_notes.text: Tritonia is a name for Minerva (the Greek Athena), linked to Lake Triton. Her 'brother' is Perseus, a half-brother through their father Jove.
'The golden shower' recalls Jove visiting Danaë as a shower of gold, which led to Perseus's birth.
Seriphus, Cythnus and Gyarus are small islands of the Cyclades in the Aegean. Minerva flies from Seriphus toward mainland Greece.
The new fountain is Hippocrene, 'horse's spring', which burst from Helicon when Pegasus struck the ground with his hoof.
Mnemonian means 'daughters of Mnemosyne' (Memory); the Muses are meant.
Daulis and Phocis were regions of central Greece near Parnassus; Pyreneus is a Thracian invader seizing them, which explains why the Muses pass through his territory.
"Mnemonian maids" means the Muses, daughters of Mnemosyne (Memory).
"Do not scruple" means do not hesitate. His closing remark that gods have entered humbler cottages is flattery meant to disarm them.
The South Wind, which brings rain, is driven off by the North Wind, which clears the sky. The Muses can now leave.
"Taking wing" is literal: the Muses escape by flying, which sets up the later bird imagery.
Magpies were known for mimicking human speech, which explains why Minerva mistakes their voices for human ones.
Pella was a city in Macedonia, and Pæonia a neighbouring region. Both place the Pierides' family in northern Greece, near the Muses' homeland.
Hæmonia is an old name for Thessaly and Achaia a region of Greece; the Pierides travelled widely through Greece to issue their challenge.
Thespian Goddesses means the Muses, linked with Thespiae near Mount Helicon in Boeotia.
The steed of Medusa is Pegasus, whose hoof struck Hippocrene spring on Helicon; Aganippe is another Muses' spring. Losers must give up these haunts.
Typhœus was a monster who attacked the gods; in this tale they fled to Egypt and disguised themselves as animals.
Ammon, the Libyan oracle god, was shown with ram's horns and identified with Jupiter, which the Pierid uses to explain the horns.
Epithets and descriptions name the gods: Delian is Apollo, son of Semele is Bacchus, sister of Phœbus is Diana, Cyllenian is Mercury.
Aonia is the region of Boeotia containing Helicon, so 'we of Aonia' means the Muses.

context_notes.text: Polydectes, king of Seriphus, had sent Perseus to fetch Medusa's head, hoping he would die. He now scorns the result.
Urania is one of the nine Muses, later associated with astronomy. Here she speaks as host on Helicon, the Muses' mountain.
Pyreneus was a king who tried to force the Muses to stay with him. The Muses go on to tell this story.
The daughter of Jupiter is Minerva (the Greek Athena), who is visiting the Muses on Mount Helicon.
Urania is the Muse of astronomy. She is answering Minerva and will go on to tell of the contest between the Muses and the daughters of Pierus.
Lucina is the goddess of childbirth, here invoked by the mother of the nine Pierides.
Pallas is Minerva, who visits the Muses and asks to hear their song.
Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry; her song, the rape of Proserpine, follows.

literary_notes.text: The narrator turns to address Polydectes directly, heightening the reproach and making his stubborn hatred feel immediate.
Polydectes denies the head's power, and his disbelief is answered by the proof that turns him to stone.
The Muse's lingering fear and mention of Pyreneus prepare the next tale of threat and violence.
Pyreneus's pious welcome hides his intent. The reader, knowing the speaker is a villain, sees the trap behind his courtesy.
His boast that he can follow wherever they go leads to his fatal leap, since he cannot fly.
The gruesome detail of the broken skull and the ground stained with blood stresses the grim punishment for his impiety.
The mimicking magpies show the punishment fitting the crime: the defeated singers become birds that merely imitate others' speech.
The narrator calls the sisters foolish for pride in their number, hinting that their boldness will lead to their downfall.
The Pierid's song glorifies Giants and belittles the gods, showing the sisters' impiety and bias.
The rapid list of gods in animal disguises is comic and undignified, which underlines the Pierid's disrespect.
Calliope's ivy-bound hair and measured playing present a dignified, skilled singer against the Pierid's 'noisy mouth' in sentence 40.
